text: Bajo Nuevo Bank, also known as the Petrel Islands (Spanish: Bajo Nuevo, Islas Petrel), is a small, uninhabited reef with some small grass-covered islets located in the western Caribbean Sea at 15°53′N 78°38′W﻿ / ﻿15.883°N 78.633°W﻿ / 15.883; -78.633, with a lighthouse on Low Cay at 15°51′N 78°38′W﻿ / ﻿15.850°N 78.633°W﻿ / 15.850; -78.633. The closest neighboring land feature is Serranilla Bank, situated 110 kilometres (68 miles) to the west. The reef was first shown on Dutch maps from 1634 and received its current name in 1654; it was rediscovered by English pirate John Glover in 1660. The area is currently involved in a sovereignty dispute among Colombia, Jamaica, and the United States. On 19 November 2012, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) unanimously ruled that the Republic of Colombia has sovereignty over both Bajo Nuevo and Serranilla Banks, although the judgment does not address the claims of Jamaica or the United States. The reef is approximately 26 km (16 mi) long and 9 km (5.6 mi) wide, featuring two distinct atoll-like structures separated by a deep channel 1.4 km (0.87 mi) wide at its narrowest point. The larger southwestern reef complex measures 15.4 km (9.6 mi) northeast-southwest and is up to 9.4 km (5.8 mi) wide, covering about 100 km² (39 sq mi), while the smaller northeastern reef complex measures 10.5 km (6.5 mi) east-west and is up to 5.5 km (3.4 mi) wide, covering 45 km² (17 sq mi). The land area is negligible. Low Cay, the most prominent cay in the southwestern atoll, is 300 m (330 yd) long and 40 m (44 yd) wide (about 1 ha or 2.5 acres), no more than 2 m (6.6 ft) high, and barren, composed of broken coral, driftwood, and sand. The lighthouse on Low Cay is a 21 m (69 ft) metal tower, painted white with a red top, emitting a focal plane beam of two white flashes every 15 seconds. The beacon was erected in 1982 and reconstructed by the Colombian Ministry of National Defence in February 2008; it is currently maintained by the Colombian National Navy and overseen by the state's Maritime Authority. Colombia currently claims the area as part of the department of San Andrés and Providencia, asserting sovereignty since 1886 as part of the geographic archipelago of San Andrés and Providencia, a claim disputed by other states who argue Colombia did not formally claim it until recently. Jamaica's claim was largely resolved through bilateral agreements with Colombia; between 1982 and 1986, a formal agreement granted regulated fishing rights to Jamaican vessels in the territorial waters of Bajo Nuevo and nearby Serranilla Bank, which critics viewed as de facto recognition of Colombian sovereignty, though the treaty expired in August 1986 and was not renewed. In November 1993, Colombia and Jamaica signed a maritime delimitation treaty establishing a "Joint Regime Area" to cooperatively manage and exploit resources in designated waters between the banks, with the territorial waters immediately surrounding the cays excluded from joint control, as Colombia considers them part of its coastal waters. The exclusion circles were defined in the treaty as "Colombia's territorial sea in Serranilla and Bajo Nuevo," despite the treaty referencing the territorial waters dispute. The agreement entered into force in March 1994. Nicaragua previously claimed all islands on its continental shelf, including Bajo Nuevo Bank and associated islands in the San Andrés and Providencia archipelagoes, covering over 50,000 km² in the Caribbean Sea, and pursued this claim in ICJ cases in 2001 and 2007, based on disputes over the validity and applicability of the Esguerr–Bárcenas treaty of March 1928. Nicaragua formally accepted the ICJ's 2012 ruling in a 2014 constitutional amendment. The United States claimed Bajo Nuevo Bank on 22 November 1869 by James W. Jennett under the Guano Islands Act; most U.S. claims over guano islands in the region were renounced in a 1972 treaty with Colombia, but Bajo Nuevo was not mentioned, and Article 7 of the treaty states that matters not specifically addressed are not bound by it. The United States considers the bank an insular area. Before ratifying a maritime boundary treaty with Colombia on 20 December 1999, Honduras had also claimed Bajo Nuevo and Serranilla Bank; in a 1986 bilateral agreement, both states excluded Honduras from control over the banks and surrounding waters, implicitly recognizing Colombian sovereignty, a position disputed by Nicaragua before the ICJ.
